title: MCP 2026-07-28: The Stateless Spec
content:
## Overview

On **2026-07-28** the Model Context Protocol shipped its largest specification revision since the protocol launched in November 2024. The headline change is a **stateless protocol core**: an MCP server no longer has to keep per-session state in memory between requests, which is what previously made horizontal scaling awkward. A follow-up roadmap published **2026-08-22** by the Core Maintainers set the direction for the next release.

This page covers what changed in the 2026-07-28 spec, why it matters for anyone running MCP servers in production, and where the protocol is heading.

---

## What Shipped in 2026-07-28

### Stateless protocol core

Earlier MCP revisions assumed a long-lived session between client and server. That works fine for a stdio server running on a laptop, but it forces sticky sessions on any HTTP deployment — every request from a client had to land on the same server process.

The stateless core removes that requirement. Requests carry the context they need, so any instance behind a load balancer can serve any request. For operators this means ordinary autoscaling instead of session-affinity routing.

### Multi Round-Trip Requests

A single logical operation can now span multiple round trips within one request lifecycle, rather than being modeled as a sequence of independent calls. This is the mechanism that lets a stateless server still handle interactions such as elicitation or sampling that inherently need more than one exchange.

### Header-based routing

Routing metadata moved into transport headers, so proxies and gateways can dispatch MCP traffic without parsing the JSON-RPC body. This is what makes MCP practical to put behind standard API-gateway infrastructure.

### Cacheable list results

`tools/list`, `resources/list`, and `prompts/list` results are now explicitly cacheable. Clients that reconnect frequently — which stateless servers encourage — no longer re-fetch an unchanged tool catalog on every connection.

### Authorization hardening

The authorization sections of the spec were tightened, closing ambiguities that had produced inconsistent implementations across servers. Enterprise deployment concerns drove much of this work.

### Formal extensions framework

Vendors can now define extensions against a defined mechanism rather than bolting proprietary fields onto core messages. This keeps the core spec small while allowing experimentation.

---

## Adoption

The Tier 1 SDKs see close to **half a billion downloads per month** combined. Both the TypeScript and Python SDKs have crossed **1 billion cumulative downloads**. All Tier 1 SDKs were updated alongside the spec release.

---

## Governance

The maintainer group expanded in 2026: **Clare Liguori** joined the Core Maintainer group, and **Den Delimarsky** joined as a Lead Maintainer. Governance maturation is one of four explicit priority areas in the roadmap.

---

## Roadmap Priorities

The 2026-08-22 roadmap organizes upcoming work into four areas:

1. **Transport evolution and scalability** — continuing the direction the stateless core opened up.
2. **Agent communication** — protocol support for agents talking to agents, not only to tools.
3. **Governance maturation** — formalizing how spec decisions get made as the contributor base grows.
4. **Enterprise readiness** — authorization, auditability, and deployment concerns.

---

## Practical Implications

If you maintain an MCP server:

- **Stateless is opt-in-shaped, not automatic.** Existing stateful servers keep working; the benefit comes from restructuring to drop per-session memory.
- **Check your list endpoints.** Advertising cacheability on a catalog that actually changes at runtime will serve clients stale tools.
- **Re-read the authorization section.** The hardening pass changed what was previously underspecified, so a "working" implementation may now be non-conformant.

If you consume MCP servers (via Claude Code, Claude Desktop, or a custom client), most of this is invisible — the payoff is servers that stay up under load and reconnect cheaply.
